titre: Two Letters Handed to a Newspaper Give Rise to the Whistleblower Test
accroche: In 2003, a Moldovan prosecutor's office official passes two letters revealing a politician's interference to a newspaper. Strasbourg draws an unprecedented test from it.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 2003, Iacob Guja heads the press service of the Prosecutor General's Office of the Republic of Moldova. Two letters, received by the Prosecutor's Office itself, concern proceedings against four police officers. In one, the Deputy Speaker of Parliament asks an official of the Prosecutor's Office to intervene personally in the case; the other, from a Deputy Minister of the Interior, recalls the past conviction of one of those officers. Guja sees in them political interference in ongoing criminal proceedings and passes them to the newspaper *Jurnal de Chișinău*, which publishes their content. On March 3, 2003, he is dismissed: the Prosecutor's Office accuses him of handing the press letters classified as secret, without consulting the heads of other departments. Neither the Prosecutor's Office nor the Deputy Speaker of Parliament appears to have disputed the authenticity of the letters. He takes the case to the European Court of Human Rights in Strasbourg, invoking Article 10 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which protects freedom of expression.

## A Test Written for the Occasion

An employee has a duty of discretion toward an employer; but the public interest can sometimes outweigh that duty. Until the judgment delivered on February 12, 2008, by the Grand Chamber in *Guja v. Moldova*, the Court had never formulated a method for deciding between the two. It builds one on this occasion: weighing together the channels used for the disclosure, the authenticity of the documents, the employee's good faith, the public interest in the information, the damage caused to the employer, and the severity of the penalty. Applying its own test, the Court notes that dismissal is the heaviest penalty possible and finds the interference not “necessary in a democratic society”: it concludes that Article 10 was violated. It is the first time it has set such criteria for the disclosure of internal information by a public official. It awards Guja 10,000 euros for damage and 8,413 euros for costs and expenses.

## The Shift

The 2008 judgment does not close the case. In 2008, the Moldovan Supreme Court orders Guja's reinstatement. Ten days later, a new dismissal order is handed to him, based on an article of the Moldovan civil service law that the Prosecutor's Office invokes because of the appointment of a new Prosecutor General. Guja returns to Strasbourg. On February 27, 2018, the Court finds a second violation of Article 10: it sees in it the continuation of the 2003 reprisals, which its own judgment had condemned ten years earlier. Fifteen years separate the dismissal from this second judgment, which finds that the State was still punishing the man the Court had protected.

repere.texte: By its Grand Chamber judgment of February 12, 2008, in *Guja v. Moldova* (application no. 14277/04), the European Court of Human Rights sets out for the first time the criteria for assessing an employee's disclosure of confidential information, and awards Iacob Guja 10,000 euros in damages and 8,413 euros in costs.
repere.source: European Court of Human Rights, Guja v. Moldova [GC], no. 14277/04, judgment of February 12, 2008

carte.punch: A civil servant passed two letters to a newspaper. Strasbourg drew an unprecedented test from it.
carte.idee: In 2003, Iacob Guja, of Moldova's Prosecutor General's Office, passes a newspaper two letters revealing a politician's interference in criminal proceedings. Dismissed, he turns to Strasbourg. On February 12, 2008, the Court sets, for the first time, six criteria for judging this kind of disclosure.

quiz.question: What does the European Court of Human Rights invent in its 2008 judgment in Guja v. Moldova?
choix: A method for assessing whether an employee who discloses confidential information can invoke freedom of expression
A European law protecting every employee who discloses confidential information
The right of a civil servant to refuse any duty of discretion toward their employer
An automatic criminal penalty against employers who dismiss a whistleblower
quiz.explication: The Court does not legislate: for the first time, it builds a six-criteria test to decide case by case between an employee's duty of discretion and the public interest in what they reveal.

quiz_supplementaire.question: On what ground does the Moldovan Prosecutor's Office dismiss Iacob Guja in 2003?
choix: For accepting a sum of money from the Deputy Speaker of the Moldovan Parliament
For refusing to carry out a written order from his direct superiors
For handing the press letters classified as secret, without consulting the other departments
For falsifying the content of the two letters before passing them to the local newspaper
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Prosecutor's Office accuses Guja of handing the press letters classified as secret, without consulting the heads of the other departments, and not of falsification, corruption, or refusing to obey.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What happens ten days after the Moldovan Supreme Court orders Guja's reinstatement in 2008?
choix: He is promoted to head the Prosecutor's Office press service
He receives a new dismissal order, based on another article of the law
He resigns of his own accord to go work at the newspaper Jurnal de Chișinău
The European Court of Human Rights itself annuls his reinstatement
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Ten days after his reinstatement, a new dismissal order is handed to him, based on an article of the Moldovan civil service law invoked after the appointment of a new Prosecutor General.

quiz_supplementaire.question: What is the total amount awarded to Guja by the Court in the 2008 judgment, damages and costs combined?
quiz_supplementaire.explication: The Court awards 10,000 euros for damage and 8,413 euros for costs and expenses, for a total of 18,413 euros.
